title: How can four squares sit symmetrically around a rectangle?
description: A rectangle of eight dots by four dots is drawn on dot paper, and four equal squares are placed one dot away diagonally from its corners. The video uses the same counts for every square and checks the result by counting from the middle.
teaching_notes: One idea: the same counts at every corner place the four squares symmetrically. Watch for children who place each square by eye, which leaves the figure uneven.

source: Draw the rectangle and four squares configuration on a dot paper. What did you do to recreate this figure so that the four squares are placed symmetrically around the rectangle? Discuss with your classmates.
video_script.why: The child uses dot counts, as in the example in the book, to place four equal squares in the same way around a rectangle.
video_script.substitution: A rectangle eight dots by four dots, with four squares of two dots by two dots, each one dot diagonally outwards from a corner.
video_script.anchor: A rectangle in the middle of a dot paper with four equal squares near its four corners, outside it and not touching it
video_script.payoff_line: The four equal squares sit alike at the four corners, one dot away diagonally.

final_answer.value: open ended; for a rectangle 8 dots wide and 4 dots tall, four squares of 2 dots by 2 dots, each placed one dot diagonally outwards from a corner of the rectangle, using the same counts every time
final_answer.spoken: the four equal squares sit alike at the four corners, one dot away diagonally; for a rectangle eight dots wide and four dots tall, each square is two dots by two dots

never_show: the finished figure before the answer
maths_rules: Rectangle corners on the dots at (0, 0), (8, 0), (8, 4) and (0, 4); it is 8 dots wide and 4 dots tall, so about twice as wide as tall.
From each corner move 1 dot diagonally outwards: the near corners of the squares are (-1, 5), (9, 5), (9, -1) and (-1, -1).

Each square is 2 dots by 2 dots and reaches away from the rectangle: top left spans x from -3 to -1 and y from 5 to 7; top right spans 9 to 11 and 5 to 7; bottom right spans 9 to 11 and -3 to -1; bottom left spans -3 to -1 and -3 to -1.
Each square is 1 dot away from the rectangle sideways and 1 dot away up or down, so it does not touch the rectangle.

Check from the middle (4, 2): the left and right squares are 5 dots away sideways to their near sides, and the top and bottom squares are 3 dots away up or down to their near sides, so the figure is symmetrical.
video_script.design: One idea: the same counts at every corner give a symmetrical figure. Uses dot counts from the example in the book. The rectangle stays all video.
open_questions: The sizes of eight dots by four dots and squares of two dots by two dots are chosen here; the book picture does not give counts.
